title: Galactic Get-Together
caption: Merging galaxies II ZW 96, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: II ZW 96 · constellation Delphinus · about 500 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, L. Armus, A. Evans

recognition.text: ESA/Webb Picture of the Month (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A galaxy merger sits at the center of this Webb image. The blue cores of two galaxies lie below center, wrapped in red star-forming regions that stretch up through and above the middle. The lower galaxy is still a mostly regular spiral, while the upper one is heavily distorted. Faint yellow diffraction spikes appear in the middle, and many tiny background galaxies are dotted across the black sky.

Cataloged as II ZW 96, the pair lies roughly 500 million light-years away in Delphinus, near the celestial equator. Their collision has given them a chaotic shape, with bright tendrils of star formation connecting their cores and the lower galaxy's arms twisted out of shape.

Those star-forming regions make the pair very bright in infrared light, which is exactly why Webb targeted it. It is one of the Luminous Infrared Galaxies, which glow more than 100 billion times as brightly as the Sun at these wavelengths.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.83 x 1.31 arcminutes) and distance (500 million light years), the frame spans roughly 266,000 × 191,000 light-years. Its light set out about 500 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This infrared image combines Webb's NIRCam and MIRI instruments. Light at 1.5 microns is shown in blue, 2.0 microns in cyan, 3.56 and 5.6 microns in green, and 4.4, 7.7 and 15 microns in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye. The colors translate wavelengths we cannot see, and the diffraction spikes come from the telescope itself.

explore: An international team proposed studying complex galaxy systems like this soon after Webb was commissioned, to test the telescope. Their targets had already been observed with Hubble and ground-based telescopes, allowing comparison.
MIRI was contributed by ESA and NASA, built by a consortium of European institutes with JPL and the University of Arizona, which also provided NIRCam.
alt: Two merging galaxies with blue cores below center, surrounded by red star-forming regions, one galaxy distorted, on a black background with many tiny galaxies.
